etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English bench, benk, bynk, from Old English benċ (“bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg-.

Cognate with Scots benk, bink (“bench”), West Frisian bank (“bench”), Dutch bank (“bench”), German Bank (“bench”), Danish bænk (“bench”), Swedish bänk (“bench”), Icelandic bekkur (“bench”). Doublet of banc, banco, and bank.

definitions.definition: A long seat with or without a back, found for example in parks and schools.

quote.citation: 2021 January 27, “Stop & Examine”, in RAIL, number 923, page 71, photo caption:
quote.text: Scarborough station's famous 139-metre-long bench, believed to be the longest in the world, has been restored in a £14,500 project.

definitions.definition: (law, figuratively) The people who decide on the verdict, collectively; the judiciary.
(law, figuratively) The office or dignity of a judge.
(law) The seat where the judges sit in court.
(government) A long seat for politicians in a parliamentary chamber.

quote.citation: 2022 April 6, Conrad Landin, “ScotRail in the public eye...”, in RAIL, number 954, page 40:
quote.text: On the opposition benches at Holyrood, Scottish Labour's transport spokesman Neil Bibby favours a more formal approach of involving passenger and worker representatives in the management of ScotRail.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) The dignity of holding an official seat.
(figuratively) The people who hold a certain type of official seat, collectively; a group of officeholders.

quote.citation: 2022 July 26, Mike Isaac, “‘Operating With Increased Intensity’: Zuckerberg Leads Meta Into Next Phase”, in The New York Times‎[1]:
quote.text: Mr. Zuckerberg’s repositioning of Meta started in earnest last year, when he began rearranging his bench of lieutenants.

definitions.definition: A seat where people sit together in an official capacity.
(sports, figuratively) The number of players on a team able to participate, expressed in terms of length.
(sports) The place where players (substitutes) and coaches sit when not playing.

quote.citation: 2011 March 1, Phil McNulty, “Chelsea 2 - 1 Man Utd”, in BBC‎[2]:
quote.text: But Chelsea, who left Didier Drogba on the bench as coach Carlo Ancelotti favoured Fernando Torres, staged a stirring fightback to move up to fourth and keep United in their sights on a night when nothing other than victory would have kept the Blues in contention.

definitions.definition: A place where assembly or hand work is performed; a workbench.
A horizontal padded surface, usually adjustable in height and inclination and often with attached weight rack, used for proper posture during exercise.

quote.citation: 2008, Lou Schuler, "Foreward", in Nate Green, Built for Show, page xii
quote.text: I had no bench or power rack, so by necessity every exercise I did started with the weights on the floor.

definitions.definition: (surveying) A bracket used to mount land surveying equipment onto a stone or a wall.[2]
A flat ledge in the slope of an earthwork, work of masonry, or similar.

quote.citation: 1912 January, Zane Grey, chapter 8, in Riders of the Purple Sage […], New York, N.Y., London: Harper & Brothers Publishers, →OCLC:
quote.text: That number carried his glance to the top of this first bulging bench of cliff-base.

definitions.definition: (geology) A thin strip of relatively flat land bounded by steeper slopes above and below.
(Australia, New Zealand) A kitchen surface on which to prepare food, a counter.
(Australia, New Zealand) A bathroom surface which holds the washbasin, a vanity.
A collection or group of dogs exhibited to the public, traditionally on benches or raised platforms.
(transitive, sports) To remove a player from play.

quote.citation: 2016, Kenneth Lonergan, Manchester by the Sea, spoken by hockey coach (Tate Donovan):
quote.text: OK, you are out! You’re benched!

definitions.definition: (transitive, figuratively) To remove someone from a position of responsibility temporarily.
(slang) To push a person backward against a conspirator behind them who is on their hands and knees, causing them to fall over.
(transitive) To furnish with benches.

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “The Flower and the Leaf: Or, The Lady in the Arbour. A Vision.”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
1847, Alfred Tennyson, “Part 2”, in The Princess: A Medley, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To place on a bench or seat of honour.

quote.citation: c. 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Winters Tale”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: whom I  […]  have benched and reared to worship

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From bench press by shortening.

definitions.definition: (transitive and intransitive, colloquial) To lift by bench pressing

quote.citation: 1988, Frederick C. Hatfield, "Powersource: Ties that bind", Ironman 47 (6): 21.
quote.text: For the first several years of my exclusive career in powerlifting, I couldn't bench too well.

definitions.definition: (weightlifting) The weight one is able to bench press, especially the maximum weight capable of being pressed.
Alternative spelling of bentsh
